newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's outspoken Franco set to take over Cenbank.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's outspoken Franco set to take over Cenbank.

text.p: Gustavo Franco, who on Tuesday looked set to take over the reins of Brazil's Central Bank, is a brainy and outspoken technocrat who is widely expected to defend the country's controversial foreign exchange policy.
Although Franco's nomination by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso still faces Senate approval, the 41-year-old economist was seen as a sure bet for the No. 1 spot at the Central Bank.
Franco would replace Gustavo Loyola, who said Tuesday he would step down for personal reasons, having completed his goal of restructuring Brazil's banking system.
While Loyola held the top post at the bank for the past two years, it was the boyish Franco who was seen as the force behind Brazil's strong foreign exchange policy.
Franco's close relationship with Cardoso has allowed him to weather sharp criticism for his insistence on maintaining a strong currency amid rising trade and current account deficits.
His frankness and forward-looking approach to economic policy -- about which he has written volumes -- also sets him apart from other members of Brazil's economic team.
"He is someone with very clear ideas. He is not someone who is going to surprise us," said Alfredo Rizkallah, president of the Sao Paulo stock exchange.

Harvard-educated and a former professor of at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, Franco was one of the architects of the Real Plan, a three year-old anti-inflation plan which succeeded in bringing Latin America's biggest economy under control.
The plan has used a strong currency and high interest rates to slash annual inflation from about 3,000 percent to single digits today.

Over the past three years, many of the economists who helped shape the Real Plan have left the government. But Franco has stayed on, earning the title of caretaker of the Plano Real, as it is known in Portuguese.
Despite his current post as International Affairs Director, he is seen by many in the market as Brazil's chief financial policy-maker.
Newspaper reports have said that such widely held perceptions have led to friction between Franco and Pedro Malan, the polished Finance Minister and Brazil's top economic spokesman.
Famous for his piercing wit, Franco was once forced to deny he referred to Malan as "Our Lady Di," in a snide comment on the Finance Minister's reported inability to formulate economic policy.
Franco's cocky style and self-assuredness has not endeared him to many of his peers.
Critics like Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor Rudiger Dornbusch say Franco's medicine of an overvalued currency and high interest rates will spell trouble down the road.
An outgoing Argentine ambassador got into hot water recently after saying the diminutive Franco was "not tall enough to see over the horizon."
